summary: A ruined 1848 stone lighthouse on a Lake Erie island off Port Maitland, dark since 1969, where a keeper and his son were lost in 1932; heritage-listed in 2015.

access.note: Reached only by boat. National Wildlife Area: visiting is prohibited 1 April to 31 August to protect nesting waterbirds (register; LighthouseFriends gives the close as 31 July). The tower is a ruin.

facts.agency: Environment Canada (Mohawk Island National Wildlife Area)

events.note: Tower completed in 1847 (LighthouseFriends); the register dates the building 1846-1848
Light first lit in spring 1848, after the lamp apparatus arrived late from England
Lamps adapted from sperm oil to coal oil
Revolving white light replaced by a group of three bright flashes
Use of a hand fog horn at the station discontinued (Department of Marine report, fiscal year ended 30 June 1901)
Double-flash long-focus reflector installed in May 1918
Unwatched Aga winter light installed, for use in the winter months
Keeper Richard Foster and his son James lost in a small skiff leaving the island in December 1932; bodies found on the shore near Port Colborne at the turn of the year (dates disputed)
Vandals landed, scaled the tower and smashed the beacon and lens
Light discontinued; a lighted buoy offshore took over
Department of Transport announced plans to demolish the abandoned tower; fishermen, boaters and residents protested
Mohawk Island National Wildlife Area created
Recognized as a Heritage Lighthouse under the Heritage Lighthouse Protection Act, 29 May 2015

corrections.why: The register calls it a lighthouse in ruins, lacking its lantern and roofs, and the Lighthouse Directory says the buildings are in ruins. The tower still stands, but its status is ruins.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The contract was let in 1846 and the tower was completed in 1847; the light was first lit in spring 1848. The register's 1846-1848 is the span of the work, and the record's 1848 is the first lighting.

notes_for_editor: Height disagrees: 18 m (59 ft) in the register, which is used in facts; about 60 feet in LighthouseFriends; 24 m (80 ft) in the Lighthouse Directory. Access season disagrees: 1 April to 31 August in the register and the Lighthouse Directory; LighthouseFriends gives 31 July in one place and 1 August in another. Distance from Port Maitland disagrees: LighthouseFriends' map gives 2.2 km (1.4 miles) offshore, its 1844 section says 'roughly five kilometres east of Port Maitland', and the Lighthouse Directory gives about 1.5 km. The story states the range and the five-kilometre passage. Keepers Smithers (R. O.) on the 1906 list (scan p.174, printed p.165) and the 1909 list (scan p.177, printed p.170) were matched by OCR line and checked on the page images: the name sits on the Mohawk Island row, and the 1909 row shows March 31, 1896 (the same row also shows April 1, 1908, not used). Burgess, J. L. Burgess, Richard H. Smithers and Foster rest on LighthouseFriends alone, apart from the 1933 dispatch which confirms Foster as keeper. The 1933 United Press dispatch (Evening Star, 2 January) disagrees with LighthouseFriends on: the son's age (21 against 25); the father's age (52 in 1933 against 'at the age of fifty' in 1921, which would make him about 61 in 1933); when the bodies were found (the dispatch has the son found the night before 2 January with the father still missing; LighthouseFriends has both found on 31 December near Point Abino); the distance from Port Colborne (2 miles against 3 miles in the newspaper LighthouseFriends quotes); and the date the pair went missing (dispatch: since 14 December; LighthouseFriends: they set off on 15 December). The story states these. The OCR of the dispatch misreads Foster as 'Poster' and the page is noisy; quotes were checked against the OCR text. The second newspaper account LighthouseFriends quotes (the son's last moments on the ice) is unidentified and is not used. LighthouseFriends names 'Richard Foster, Jr.' among the two men who rowed to the island; because the family relation is unclear, the story names only Ovide Charette. The 1844 plea, the blanket anecdote, the 1864 coal oil change and the 1889 and 1918 characteristic changes come from LighthouseFriends alone. The register names John B. McIntyre as architect or designer, while John Brown is the builder; the story reports the register's listing and says the sources do not say what McIntyre did. The Lighthouse Directory says the owner is unknown; the record's ownership 'federal' is not stated in the sources read, so it is left out of facts. The fire the Lighthouse Directory mentions has no date and is not in the events list. The 1977 creation of the National Wildlife Area is from LighthouseFriends alone; the register and heritage statement do not date it. The record's access 'closed' is recorded as 'restricted' in facts, since the island is closed only in the nesting season and the tower is a ruin. Six chapters for rich evidence. The story is about 1,350 words, within the rich range.
